clips.send: Ural Mountains. The boundary between Europe and Asia. Run about 2,500 km north to south through western Russia, from the Arctic toward Kazakhstan. The traditional dividing line between Europe (west) and Asia (east). Very old and worn down by erosion; the highest peak is only 1,895 m. Rich in iron, copper, coal and gemstones; industrial cities such as Yekaterinburg grew here.

clips.send: Russia. The largest country on Earth. About 17 million square kilometers , spanning Europe and Asia and 11 time zones; the Ural Mountains divide the two parts. Most people live in the European part, west of the Urals, where the climate is milder. Long, very cold winters; much of Siberia is frozen permafrost. Huge reserves of oil, natural gas, timber and minerals — energy is its main export.

clips.send: Air pollution in the UK. From coal smog to traffic fumes. Britain was the first country to industrialize, burning coal in factories and homes. The Great Smog of London (December 1952) lasted five days and killed thousands of people. The Clean Air Act of 1956 banned smoky fuels in cities. Today traffic exhaust is the main problem; London’s Ultra Low Emission Zone charges polluting cars.

clips.send: Black Forest. Wooded mountains in south-west Germany. In the 1980s acid rain killed many of its trees, which led to cleaner power plants and cars.

clips.send: United Kingdom. An island nation off north-west Europe. England, Scotland and Wales (on Great Britain) plus Northern Ireland; the English Channel separates it from France. Mild and rainy all year thanks to the North Atlantic Drift and westerly winds. Birthplace of the Industrial Revolution (coal and iron); North Sea oil and gas; London is a world financial centre. Issue: air pollution — from the deadly coal smog of 1952 to today’s traffic fumes.

clips.send: Chernobyl. In 1986 a reactor at the nuclear power plant here exploded, spreading radioactive dust over much of Europe. A 30-km zone around it is still closed.

clips.send: London. William the Conqueror began the Tower of London. Later London was the heart of the English Revolution, the Industrial Revolution and a huge empire.

clips.send: Hudson Bay. A huge, shallow sea in northern Canada that freezes over every winter. Polar bears wait on its shores for the ice to come back.
clips.text: Hudson Bay. A huge, shallow sea in northern Canada that freezes over every winter. Polar bears wait on its shores for the ice to come back.

clips.send: North European Plain. Europe’s great flat lowland. Europe’s largest landform: a wide, flat lowland stretching from France through Belgium, Germany and Poland into Russia. Fertile soils grow wheat, potatoes and sugar beets — Europe’s “breadbasket”. Many big cities (Paris, Berlin, Warsaw, Moscow) and a dense population lie on it; rivers such as the Rhine, Elbe and Vistula cross it. Being flat made it easy for trade — and for armies to invade.

clips.send: Scandinavian Peninsula. Europe’s largest peninsula, home to Norway and Sweden: deep fjords on the Atlantic side, gentler land on the Baltic side.

clips.send: Italy. The boot-shaped peninsula. A peninsula reaching into the Mediterranean; the Alps in the north, the Apennines running down its length. Mediterranean climate — olives, grapes and citrus; active volcanoes Vesuvius and Etna. The fertile Po Valley in the north holds most farms and factories (cars, fashion, machines). Heart of the ancient Roman Empire; tourism is a huge industry.

clips.send: Scandinavian Peninsula. Norway and Sweden’s northern peninsula. Europe’s largest peninsula, home to Norway, Sweden and part of Finland, between the Atlantic and the Baltic Sea. Ice-age glaciers carved Norway’s coast into deep, narrow sea inlets called fjords. The far north lies above the Arctic Circle (midnight sun in summer), but the warm North Atlantic Drift keeps Norway’s ports ice-free. North Sea oil and gas, hydropower, timber, iron ore and fishing.
